items.title: Humboldt Group Awarded State Tourism Grant
items.summary: A Humboldt organization is awarded a state tourism grant for marketing. The organization called A Bolder Humboldt will share in a part of $117,408 through the Kansas Department of Commerce to market the City, reach new audiences, and inspire visitors to explore the Sunflower State. A Bolder Humboldt's ongoing efforts to revitalize the City have included a new brewery, hotels, a campground, bars, restaurants, a candy shop, and a music venue among other attractions. The new grant will provide the group with an additional ten-thousand dollars ($10,000) to bring new visitors to southeast Kansas. Humboldt is one of 18 communities to receive a Kansas Tourism Marketing grant.

items.title: Longtime KGGF General Manager to Retire
items.summary: After more than 30 years as General Manager, KGGF's John Leonard will retire on Friday. Leonard's voice has been a staple of life in southeast Kansas and Northeast Oklahoma, and he says his journey to this area started in 1980 when he came to Pawhuska to work a 6-month job at a station there. While Leonard says it's been a long 6 months, he eventually made his way to the KGGF airwaves, working in the news department. Leonard eventually came back to KGGF as General Manager in 1996 and says he grew to love the sales side of the industry and helping local businesses grow. Looking back on his career, Leonard says the station's service during the 2007 flood sticks out. In Retirement, Leonard will be moving to Oklahoma City, but he still plans to visit Coffeyville and continue doing voice-over work for the station, in addition to enjoying his newfound hobby of music and guitar playing. Listeners are invited to a farewell celebration on Friday, October 30th from 10 to 1 p.m. at the KGGF Studios located at 306 W 8 th Street in Coffeyville. items.title: New Laws to Go Into Effect in Oklahoma on Sunday
items.summary: Two new Oklahoma laws aimed at improving public safety take effect November 1 st . Republican Representative Steve Bashore of Miami authored both measures. House Bill 3244 strengthens penalties for organized retail crime and identity theft. It expands the types of personal information covered under identity theft laws, including fingerprints, passwords and PIN numbers. The measure also increases penalties for repeat offenders and closes loopholes that allow criminals to exploit vulnerable people, including seniors and minors. House Bill 2941 requires first responders to notify law enforcement when they suspect a drug overdose, after addressing the patient's immediate medical needs. It also establishes fentanyl as the presumed cause of death in fatal overdoses involving the drug. The Oklahoma State Department of Health reports fentanyl was involved in 86 percent of opioid-related overdose deaths in 2024. Bashore says both laws are designed to protect Oklahomans by holding criminals accountable and helping authorities better track and respond to the state's growing fentanyl problem.

It preserves a connection between generations of Quapaw families, the early development of Catholicism in northeastern Oklahoma, and a mission whose legacy extended far beyond its closing nearly a century ago. items.title: 43rd Annual Pelican Festival at Grand Lake
items.summary: Grand Lake welcomes the pelicans back as 43rd annual festival returns to Grove GROVE, Okla. — One of northeast Oklahoma’s most recognizable signs of autumn is returning to Grand Lake — and this weekend, an entire festival is being held in its honor. The 43rd Annual Pelican Festival runs Thursday through Sunday, Oct. 1-4, at Wolf Creek Park in Grove, bringing together carnival rides, live music, food trucks, arts and crafts, classic vehicles and excursions onto Grand Lake to see the enormous white birds that inspired the celebration. The festival is organized around the seasonal migration of the American White Pelican, which passes through the Grand Lake region during the spring and fall. Festival organizers say the birds can be seen around the lake from roughly September through November during their fall movement. They are difficult birds to overlook. American White Pelicans are among the largest flying birds in North America. items.title: Before "Sooner"
items.summary: Before “Sooner” Became a Namesake of Pride: Indian Territory, the Land Runs, and the Making of Modern-Day Oklahoma The word “Sooner” is now inseparable from Oklahoma identity. Its original meaning was considerably different. The first Sooners were people who entered land before the federal government legally opened it for settlement, violating rules designed to give prospective claimants an equal starting time. The land itself lay within Indian Territory, amid treaty-established Native nations whose governments, boundaries, and property rights had developed through removal, war, negotiated agreements, federal coercion, and decades of political struggle. I. Oklahoma Did Not Begin With the Land Run At noon on April 22, 1889, thousands of people surged into approximately 1.9 million acres in central Indian Territory. The event became one of the enduring images of Oklahoma history: horses running across prairie, wagons bouncing over rough ground, railroad passengers pouring into improvised towns, and homesteaders driving stakes into the earth. items.summary: Dustin Allen Brings Prosecutor, Public Defender Experience to Tulsa County Judge Race TULSA COUNTY, Okla. — Voters in Tulsa County’s Judicial District 14, Office 4, will choose between attorney Dustin Allen and Special Judge Loretta Radford on Nov. 3, following a three-candidate June election that also included prosecutor Phillip Peak. The Oklahoma State Election Board’s November ballot confirms Allen and Radford as the remaining candidates for the nonpartisan judicial seat. For Allen, the campaign presents voters with a somewhat unusual combination of experience from both sides of Oklahoma’s criminal justice system. He has worked as a prosecutor, served as an assistant public defender, built a private trial practice, and operated his own law firm for more than a decade. His campaign says that experience informs a judicial philosophy centered on applying statutes and the Constitution as written, maintaining public safety, moving cases efficiently, and treating litigants with respect. items.title: WHEN THE GOVERNMENT BECOMES PART OF THE DRUG TRANSACTION
items.summary: WHEN THE GOVERNMENT BECOMES PART OF THE DRUG TRADE Controlled buys, informants and controlled deliveries can expose criminal networks. Documented cases also show what happens when the line between investigation and participation breaks down. There is an uncomfortable paradox at the center of modern narcotics enforcement. Government exists, in part, to prevent dangerous drugs from reaching the public, yet some of the investigative techniques used to accomplish that purpose necessarily place police officers, confidential informants, money, firearms, and sometimes controlled substances inside the very commerce government is attempting to suppress. A confidential informant may be instructed to purchase fentanyl. An undercover operative may negotiate a drug transaction. Investigators may permit a package of apparent narcotics to continue toward its destination so that they can identify the recipient. Police may conduct a controlled sale or delivery rather than immediately terminate a transaction. Each practice can produce evidence that would otherwise be difficult to obtain.
